# Bounds methods [✎ Draft]{.badge .badge-draft2} {#sec-bounds}

```{r}
#| include: false
if(file.exists("../_setup.R")){source("../_setup.R")}
```

The methods in this chapter rest on the properties of bounded data described in @sec-bounded-data: on a scale with a minimum and a maximum, the mean and the *SD* are not free to take any values independently of one another.

## Mean inside range {#sec-mean-inside-range}

The simplest bounds check is whether a mean lies within the range of values that its scores could take. The mean of a single item rated from 1 to 5 must lie between 1 and 5. The range of a sum score is the number of items multiplied by the lowest and highest response options, so six items rated from 1 to 5 give sum scores from 6 to 30, and their mean must lie between 6 and 30. A percentage must lie between 0 and 100. When an article reports the smallest and largest observed scores, the mean must also lie between those. And a mean exactly at the minimum or maximum is only possible if every participant had that score, in which case the *SD* must be zero (@sec-mean-sd-bounded).

Working out the range requires knowing the number of items, the response options, how they were coded (for example, from 0 or from 1), and whether items were summed or averaged. Articles sometimes describe these inconsistently, so a mean outside the range shows that either the mean or the description of the measure is wrong, without saying which.

The same reasoning applies to the means of subgroups. When the subgroups together make up the whole sample, without overlap, the mean of the whole sample is a weighted average of the subgroup means, so it must lie between the smallest and the largest of them. The same is true of percentages.

@haller2022 reported the characteristics of 9,496 participants in their Table 1, both for the whole sample and for eight regions, whose sample sizes add up to 9,496. In the whole sample, 5.1% of participants were divorced, but the table reports 0.0% divorced in every one of the eight regions. Likewise, 5.5% of the whole sample lived with friends or roommates, but 0.0% in every region. A percentage for the whole sample cannot be larger than the percentages in all of the groups that make it up, so these rows of the table cannot be correct. The regression in the same article's Table 5 includes being divorced and living with friends or roommates as predictors, with estimated coefficients, which suggests that participants in these groups did exist and that the regional zeros are the error.

The same article also describes the ranges of two of its measures inconsistently. The sum score of six prosocial behaviour items, each rated from 1 to 5, is described as ranging from 6 to 36 in the Method section, but from 6 to 30 in Table 4, which is correct. The fourteen well-being items are described as rated on a "6-point" scale from 0 to 6, which has seven points, while the range of the sum score is given as 0 to 70, which is only possible if each item was scored from 0 to 5. None of these means falls outside its range, but the inconsistencies show why the range of a measure should be worked out from its items, not taken from the article.

## SD bounds {#sec-sd-bounds}

On a bounded scale, the mean and the *SD* are not free to vary independently of one another (@sec-mean-sd-bounded). The scale's minimum and maximum, the sample size, and the mean together set an upper bound on the *SD*, and once the data are known to be whole numbers, or to include a particular minimum and maximum, they set a lower bound too. A reported *SD* outside these bounds cannot be correct. @hussey2026brimmer call this check BRIMMER, for Bounds-Related Inconsistency of Means and Errors Reported, by analogy with GRIMMER (@sec-grimmer). Its counterpart for the mean alone, BRIM, asks whether the reported mean can be reached at all, as in @sec-mean-inside-range.

The bounds come from a series of nested constraints, each of which can only tighten them [@hussey2026brimmer]:

- **The scale limits.** The most spread out any set of scores can be is half at the minimum and half at the maximum. On a scale with range *R*, the sample *SD* can never exceed *R* / √2, which is reached by a sample of two people, one at each end.
- **The sample size.** With more people, the largest possible *SD* falls towards *R* / 2. For an even sample size it is (*R* / 2) × √(*n* / (*n* − 1)), and for an odd one slightly less, because the people cannot be split evenly between the two ends [@popoviciu1935]. On a 1–7 scale with 30 people, no *SD* can exceed 3.05, whatever the mean.
- **The mean.** The further the mean is from the middle of the scale, the smaller the largest possible *SD*, which is √(*n* / (*n* − 1) × (*max* − *M*)(*M* − *min*)). This is the Bhatia–Davis bound of @sec-mean-sd-bounded, which @muilwijk1966 had already derived [@bhatia2000]. It can be sharpened slightly, because the number of people at each end of the scale must be a whole number. On a 1–7 scale with 30 people and a mean of 2.97, the *SD* can be at most 2.84.
- **Integer data.** Up to this point, the smallest possible *SD* is zero: everyone could have the same score. But when every response is a whole number, a mean with a fractional part, such as 2.97, cannot be produced by identical scores, so the *SD* must be above zero. This floor is usually small: 0.14 in the example.
- **Internal consistency.** For a score made up of several items, a reported Cronbach's α limits how much the items can disagree with one another, which lowers the ceiling and, for whole-number items, raises the floor [@hussey2026brimmer].

The scale limits are not the only minimum and maximum that constrain the *SD*. Many articles report the smallest and largest scores actually observed, in a table of descriptive statistics or in the text, and these say more than the scale limits do. The scale limits only say that no score lies outside them, whereas an observed minimum and maximum say that at least one person had each of those scores. A sample that includes both a low and a high score cannot have a very small *SD*, so the observed minimum and maximum raise the floor substantially, especially together with the mean and integer data. They also narrow the range of means that are possible at all, and they lower the ceiling, because the observed range is usually narrower than the scale's. In the example above, if the article also reported that scores ranged from 1 to 6, the *SD* could be no smaller than 0.71 and no larger than 2.46.

When checking reported values, the bounds have to take rounding into account: a mean reported as 2.97 could have been anything from 2.965 to 2.975, and the bounds are calculated over that whole interval. Like GRIM and GRIMMER, BRIMMER is a necessary condition rather than a sufficient one. A reported *SD* outside the bounds is impossible, but one inside them may still not correspond to any real set of whole-number scores. How the bounds combine with the granularity checks, and a further, exact test, BRIMMEST, which settles whether any such set of scores exists, are the subject of @sec-combined [@hussey2026brimmer].

Put the two constraints together, and the mean and the *SD* carry information about one another. When the scores are whole numbers and the scale has a minimum and a maximum, knowing the mean limits what the *SD* can be, and knowing the *SD* limits what the mean can be. Together, they also limit the distributions of scores that could have produced them: a large *SD* means that the scores must be piled up near the ends of the scale, and a small one means that they must be bunched together, and in a small sample a mean and *SD* can leave only one or a few sets of scores that produce them. Neither constraint is enough on its own. Continuous data on a bounded scale can take any *SD* between zero and the ceiling, and whole-number data without a minimum or maximum are subject only to the granularity constraints of @sec-granularity, which say nothing about how large the *SD* can be.

The plot below shows this in the simplest case: a single item answered in whole numbers, with a small sample on a short scale, so that every set of scores that could have been observed can be listed. Each dot on the left is a combination of mean and *SD* that at least one set of scores produces, and the shaded band runs from the smallest to the largest possible *SD* at each mean, from the bounds above. The dotted curve is the uniform-spread bound from @sec-mean-sd-bounded: above it, the scores are more spread out than if they were spread evenly across the whole scale. Click or drag in the plot to choose a combination: the choice snaps to the nearest dot, and the plot on the right shows the frequencies of a set of scores that produces it. When more than one set does, **Show another** steps through them.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ssMin = Inputs.number({value: 1, step: 1, label: "Scale minimum"})
viewof ssMax = Inputs.number({value: 5, step: 1, label: "Scale maximum"})
viewof ssN = Inputs.range([2, 12], {value: 8, step: 1, label: "Sample size (n)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// every set of n whole-number scores on the scale, grouped by the mean and SD it gives. with at most 7 response
// options and 12 people there are at most 18,564 sets, so they can all be listed
ssSets = {
  if (!(Number.isInteger(ssMin) && Number.isInteger(ssMax) && ssMax > ssMin && ssMax - ssMin <= 6)) return null
  const k = ssMax - ssMin + 1, n = ssN, groups = new Map(), counts = new Array(k).fill(0)
  const add = () => {
    // the sum and sum of squares, counted from the scale minimum, identify the mean and SD exactly
    let S = 0, Q = 0
    for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) { S += i * counts[i]; Q += i * i * counts[i] }
    const key = S * 1000 + Q
    if (!groups.has(key)) groups.set(key, {key, mean: ssMin + S / n, sd: Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, (Q - S * S / n) / (n - 1))), sets: []})
    groups.get(key).sets.push(counts.slice())
  }
  const fill = (i, left) => {
    if (i === k - 1) { counts[i] = left; add(); return }
    for (let c = left; c >= 0; c--) { counts[i] = c; fill(i + 1, left - c) }
  }
  fill(0, n)
  return {k, n, l: ssMin, u: ssMax, points: [...groups.values()]}
}

// the chosen mean and SD. it is kept when the scale or sample size changes, and snapped to the nearest possible dot
mutable ssPick = null

// the latest plot's scales and dots, so that a drag that began on an earlier version of it is converted with the current one
ssDrag = ({x: null, y: null, points: null, key: null})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  if (!ssSets) return html`<div class="sc-status">Set the minimum and maximum to whole numbers, with the maximum between 1 and 6 above the minimum.</div>`
  const {n, l, u, points} = ssSets, R = u - l
  const target = ssPick ?? {mean: l + 0.4 * R, sd: R / 4}
  const chosen = d3.least(points, p => (p.mean - target.mean) ** 2 + (p.sd - target.sd) ** 2)
  const colour = "#e8710a", fmt = x => x.toFixed(2)

  const twoCol = width >= 640, gap = 32
  const w = twoCol ? Math.floor((width - gap) / 2) : width, height = 340
  const step = R / 600
  // the uniform-spread bound is the Bhatia-Davis bound scaled down by 1 / sqrt(3), as in the explorer below
  const curve = d3.range(l, u + step / 2, step).map(m => ({m, floor: sxQuasiFloor(m, n), ceiling: sxCeiling(m, n, l, u),
    uniform: Math.sqrt(n / (n - 1) * Math.max(0, (u - m) * (m - l)) / 3)}))
  const r = points.length > 1000 ? 1.5 : points.length > 300 ? 2 : 2.8

  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: w, height, marginLeft: 50, marginRight: 15, marginTop: 15, marginBottom: 45,
    x: {label: "Mean", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36, domain: [l, u]},
    y: {label: "SD", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 40, domain: [0, 1.05 * sxParityMax(l, u, n)], grid: true},
    style: {fontSize: "13px"},
    marks: [
      Plot.areaY(curve, {x: "m", y1: "floor", y2: "ceiling", fill: "#2780e3", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
      Plot.line(curve, {x: "m", y: "ceiling", stroke: "#2780e3", strokeWidth: 1.2}),
      Plot.line(curve, {x: "m", y: "floor", stroke: "#2780e3", strokeWidth: 1.2}),
      Plot.line(curve, {x: "m", y: "uniform", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.6, strokeDasharray: "1,3", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
      Plot.dot(points, {x: "mean", y: "sd", r, fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.6}),
      Plot.ruleX([chosen.mean], {y1: 0, y2: chosen.sd, stroke: colour, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.dot([chosen], {x: "mean", y: "sd", r: 7, fill: colour, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 1.5})
    ]
  })

  // clicking or dragging in the plot chooses the nearest possible combination, measured on the screen
  Object.assign(ssDrag, {x: plot.scale("x"), y: plot.scale("y"), points, key: chosen.key})
  plot.style.cursor = "crosshair"
  plot.style.touchAction = "none"
  plot.addEventListener("pointerdown", down => {
    const box = plot.getBoundingClientRect()
    const pick = event => {
      const px = (event.clientX - box.left) * w / box.width, py = (event.clientY - box.top) * height / box.height
      const p = d3.least(ssDrag.points, d => (ssDrag.x.apply(d.mean) - px) ** 2 + (ssDrag.y.apply(d.sd) - py) ** 2)
      if (p.key !== ssDrag.key) { ssDrag.key = p.key; mutable ssPick = {mean: p.mean, sd: p.sd} }
    }
    down.preventDefault()
    pick(down)
    let pending = null
    const move = event => {
      if (pending === null) requestAnimationFrame(() => { pick(pending); pending = null })
      pending = event
    }
    const up = () => {
      window.removeEventListener("pointermove", move)
      window.removeEventListener("pointerup", up)
      window.removeEventListener("pointercancel", up)
    }
    window.addEventListener("pointermove", move)
    window.addEventListener("pointerup", up)
    window.addEventListener("pointercancel", up)
  })

  // the frequencies of one set of scores with the chosen mean and SD, with a button to step through the others
  const sets = chosen.sets, values = d3.range(l, u + 1)
  let index = 0
  const right = html`<div style="width: ${w}px; max-width: 100%;"></div>`
  const draw = () => {
    const data = values.map((value, i) => ({value, count: sets[index][i]}))
    const bars = Plot.plot({
      width: w, height, marginLeft: 50, marginRight: 15, marginTop: 15, marginBottom: 45,
      x: {label: "Response", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36, domain: [l - 0.5, u + 0.5], ticks: values, tickFormat: "d"},
      y: {label: "Frequency", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 40, domain: [0, n], grid: true, ticks: Math.min(n, 6), tickFormat: "d"},
      style: {fontSize: "13px"},
      marks: [
        Plot.rectY(data, {x1: d => d.value - 0.42, x2: d => d.value + 0.42, y: "count", fill: colour, fillOpacity: 0.55}),
        Plot.text(data, {x: "value", y: "count", text: d => d.count, dy: -8, fontSize: 12}),
        Plot.ruleY([0]),
        // the mean, in the same colour as the chosen point on the left
        Plot.ruleX([chosen.mean], {stroke: colour, strokeWidth: 2.5, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
        Plot.text([chosen.mean], {x: d => d, frameAnchor: "top", dy: -2, text: d => `Mean ${fmt(d)}`, fill: colour, fontWeight: 600, fontSize: 12, textAnchor: "start", dx: 5})
      ]
    })
    const button = html`<button class="btn btn-quarto btn-sm" style="margin: 0; white-space: nowrap;">Show another</button>`
    button.onclick = () => { index = (index + 1) % sets.length; draw() }
    right.replaceChildren(
      html`<div style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; gap: 1rem; min-height: 2.4rem; font-weight: 600;">
        <span>${sets.length === 1 ? "The only set of scores with this mean and " : `Set ${index + 1} of ${sets.length} with this mean and `}<i>SD</i></span>${sets.length > 1 ? button : ""}</div>`,
      bars)
  }
  draw()

  const left = html`<div style="width: ${w}px; max-width: 100%;"><div style="display: flex; align-items: center; min-height: 2.4rem; font-weight: 600;"><span>Possible means and <i>SD</i>s</span></div>${plot}</div>`
  const feedback = html`<div class="sb-feedback sb-feedback-ok">`
  feedback.innerHTML = `<strong>Mean ${fmt(chosen.mean)}, <em>SD</em> ${fmt(chosen.sd)}.</strong> ${sets.length === 1 ? "Exactly one set" : `${sets.length} different sets`} of ${n} whole-number scores from ${l} to ${u} ${sets.length === 1 ? "gives" : "give"} this mean and <em>SD</em>. Altogether, samples of ${n} on this scale can produce ${points.length} different combinations of mean and <em>SD</em>.`
  const legend = html`<div class="bd-legend">
    <span><svg width="28" height="12"><rect width="28" height="12" fill="#2780e3" fill-opacity="0.12"/><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="1" y2="1" stroke="#2780e3" stroke-width="1.2"/></svg> Bounds</span>
    <span><svg width="12" height="12"><circle cx="6" cy="6" r="2.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.6"/></svg> Possible with whole numbers</span>
    <span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.6" stroke-dasharray="1,3" stroke-width="1.5"/></svg> Uniform-spread bound</span>
  </div>`
  left.append(legend)
  return html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.5rem ${gap}px; align-items: flex-start;">${left}${right}</div>${feedback}`
}
```

Three things stand out. First, the dots fill the band only patchily. A mean and an *SD* inside the bounds need not be produced by any set of whole-number scores, which is why the bounds are a necessary condition rather than a sufficient one, and why the granularity checks of @sec-granularity add to them. Second, the dots along the top edge of the band are the most spread out samples possible at each mean: choose one, and the scores on the right sit at the two ends of the scale, with at most one person in between. The dots along the bottom edge are the least spread out, with everyone on one response or two neighbouring ones. Increase the sample size, or widen the scale, and the dots crowd together, until they are too many to tell apart. This is why, in practice, the bounds are calculated rather than every possible sample being listed. Third, the mean and *SD* say a good deal about the shape of the data. Choose a dot above the uniform-spread bound, and the scores that produce it are piled up towards the ends of the scale. Choose one near the floor, and the scores are bunched on neighbouring responses. With a small sample, many dots are produced by only one set of scores, so the mean and *SD* alone are enough to recover every score.

The next plot drops these restrictions and shows the bounds for any scale, sample size, and mean. The shaded band shows the combinations of mean and *SD* that are possible. Move the sliders, or click or drag anywhere in the plot, to choose a mean and an *SD*, and the point shows whether that combination is possible. Choose whether responses are continuous or whole numbers, and whether the score is a single item, or the sum or mean of several items, each rated on the scale. For a score made up of several items, tick **Cronbach's α** to add a reported α. Tick **Observed minimum and maximum** to see how much a reported minimum and maximum sharpen the bounds; these are in the units of the score. The dashed grey curve is the Bhatia–Davis bound, which ignores that people come in whole numbers, and the dotted horizontal line is the largest *SD* that any sample of this size can have, whatever its mean. The dotted curve is the uniform-spread bound from @sec-mean-sd-bounded. It is not a bound on what is possible, but on what is plausible: above it, the scores are more spread out than if they were spread evenly across the whole scale, which requires them to pile up at its ends. This plot shows the bounds only. It treats the mean and *SD* as exact, does not allow for rounding, and does not check granularity, so it does not ask whether a mean or *SD* could have come from whole-number data at all, as GRIM and GRIMMER do (@sec-granularity). It is for building intuition about the bounds. To check values reported in an article, use the app in @sec-combined-app, which combines the bounds with the granularity checks.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sxMin = Inputs.number({value: 1, step: 1, label: "Scale minimum"})
viewof sxMax = Inputs.number({value: 7, step: 1, label: "Scale maximum"})
viewof sxN = Inputs.range([2, 100], {value: 30, step: 1, label: "Sample size (n)"})
viewof sxZ = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Continuous", "continuous"], ["Whole numbers", "quasiinteger"]]), {value: "quasiinteger", label: "Responses"})
viewof sxScoring = Inputs.radio(new Map([["A single item", "single"], ["A sum of items", "sum"], ["A mean of items", "mean"]]), {value: "single", label: "Score"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sxK = Inputs.range([2, 20], {value: 3, step: 1, label: "Number of items", disabled: sxScoring === "single"})
viewof sxUseAlpha = Inputs.toggle({label: "Cronbach's α", value: false, disabled: sxScoring === "single"})
viewof sxAlpha = Inputs.range([0, 0.99], {value: 0.8, step: 0.01, label: "α", disabled: sxScoring === "single" || !sxUseAlpha})
viewof sxUseAB = Inputs.toggle({label: "Observed minimum and maximum", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// the score's units: a sum of k items runs from k times the scale minimum to k times its maximum
sxItems = sxScoring === "single" ? 1 : sxK
sxBounds = Number.isFinite(sxMin) && Number.isFinite(sxMax) && sxMax > sxMin
  ? (sxScoring === "sum" ? [sxMin * sxItems, sxMax * sxItems] : [sxMin, sxMax]) : null
// the observed extremes start just inside the scale, and can only be changed while they are in use
viewof sxA = Inputs.number({value: (sxBounds ?? [1, 7])[0], step: 1, label: "Observed minimum", disabled: !sxUseAB})
viewof sxB = Inputs.number({value: (sxBounds ?? [1, 7])[1] - 1, step: 1, label: "Observed maximum", disabled: !sxUseAB})
// the slider steps follow the scale: 0.01 on a 1 to 7 scale, 1 on a 0 to 1000 scale
viewof sxMean = {
  const [lo, hi] = sxBounds ?? [1, 7], range = hi - lo, step = 10 ** (Math.floor(Math.log10(range)) - 2)
  return Inputs.range([lo, hi], {value: lo + Math.round(0.33 * range / step) * step, step, label: "Mean"})
}
viewof sxSd = {
  const [lo, hi] = sxBounds ?? [1, 7], range = hi - lo, step = 10 ** (Math.floor(Math.log10(range)) - 2)
  return Inputs.range([0, Math.floor(range / Math.SQRT2 / step) * step], {value: Math.round(range / 4 / step) * step, step, label: "SD"})
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  if (!sxBounds) return html`<div class="sc-status">Set the minimum and maximum to numbers, with the minimum below the maximum.</div>`
  const [l, u] = sxBounds, n = sxN
  const design = {n, k: sxItems, quasi: sxZ === "quasiinteger", toSum: sxScoring === "mean" ? sxItems : 1, itemLimits: [sxMin, sxMax],
    alpha: sxScoring !== "single" && sxUseAlpha ? sxAlpha : null}
  const abValid = sxUseAB && Number.isFinite(sxA) && Number.isFinite(sxB) && sxA >= l && sxB <= u && sxB > sxA
  const abProblem = sxUseAB && !abValid ? "The observed minimum and maximum must be numbers within the range of the score, with the minimum below the maximum." : null
  design.ab = abValid ? [sxA, sxB] : null
  const at = m => sxBoundsAt(m, design)
  const here = at(sxMean)

  // a grid fine enough to show the steps of the whole-number floor
  const range = u - l
  const step = Math.max(range / 4000, Math.min(range / 800, 1 / (4 * n * design.toSum)))
  const bd = m => Math.sqrt(n / (n - 1) * Math.max(0, (u - m) * (m - l)))
  const curve = d3.range(l, u + step / 2, step).map(m => ({m, ...at(m), bd: bd(m), uniform: bd(m) / Math.sqrt(3)}))
  // with alpha or observed extremes, the bounds from the scale limits alone are drawn for comparison
  const sharpened = design.alpha !== null || design.ab !== null
  const reference = sharpened ? curve.map(d => ({m: d.m, ...sxBoundsAt(d.m, {...design, alpha: null, ab: null})})) : null
  const anyMax = sxParityMax(l, u, n)
  const yMax = 1.1 * Math.max(anyMax, sxSd)
  const verdict = sxVerdict(sxMean, sxSd, here, design, bd(sxMean) / Math.sqrt(3))
  const colour = {ok: "#3b9c6e", warn: "#d9a02b", bad: "#c0392b"}[verdict.kind]
  const fmt = (x, d = 2) => Number.isFinite(x) ? x.toFixed(d) : "—"

  const marginLeft = 50, marginRight = 20, marginTop = 15, marginBottom = 45, height = 380
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width, height, marginLeft, marginRight, marginTop, marginBottom,
    x: {label: sxScoring === "sum" ? "Mean (sum score)" : sxScoring === "mean" ? "Mean (mean of items)" : "Mean", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36, domain: [l, u]},
    y: {label: "SD", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 40, domain: [0, yMax], grid: true},
    style: {fontSize: "13px"},
    marks: [
      Plot.areaY(curve, {x: "m", y1: "floor", y2: "ceiling", fill: "#2780e3", fillOpacity: 0.18}),
      reference ? Plot.line(reference, {x: "m", y: "ceiling", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.35, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}) : null,
      reference ? Plot.line(reference, {x: "m", y: "floor", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.35, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}) : null,
      reference ? null : Plot.line(curve, {x: "m", y: "bd", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.45, strokeDasharray: "6,4"}),
      Plot.line(curve, {x: "m", y: "uniform", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.6, strokeDasharray: "1,3", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      Plot.line(curve, {x: "m", y: "ceiling", stroke: "#2780e3", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      Plot.line(curve, {x: "m", y: "floor", stroke: "#2780e3", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      Plot.ruleY([anyMax], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.5, strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
      Plot.text([`Largest SD at any mean: ${fmt(anyMax)}`], {x: (l + u) / 2, y: anyMax, dy: -8, fontSize: 11, fillOpacity: 0.7}),
      design.ab ? Plot.ruleX(sxMeanBand(n, ...design.ab), {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.5, strokeDasharray: "2,3"}) : null,
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
      Plot.ruleX([sxMean], {y1: 0, y2: sxSd, stroke: colour, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.dot([{}], {x: sxMean, y: sxSd, r: 7, fill: colour, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 1.5})
    ]
  })
  // clicking anywhere in the plot moves the sliders to that mean and SD, and dragging moves them continuously. the plot
  // is redrawn at every change, so the drag is followed on the window, with the latest plot's scales
  sxDrag.x = plot.scale("x"); sxDrag.y = plot.scale("y")
  plot.style.cursor = "crosshair"
  plot.style.touchAction = "none"
  plot.addEventListener("pointerdown", down => {
    const box = plot.getBoundingClientRect()
    const pick = event => {
      const px = (event.clientX - box.left) * width / box.width, py = (event.clientY - box.top) * height / box.height
      sxSet(viewof sxMean, sxDrag.x.invert(px))
      sxSet(viewof sxSd, sxDrag.y.invert(py))
    }
    down.preventDefault()
    pick(down)
    let pending = null
    const move = event => {
      if (pending === null) requestAnimationFrame(() => { pick(pending); pending = null })
      pending = event
    }
    const up = () => {
      window.removeEventListener("pointermove", move)
      window.removeEventListener("pointerup", up)
      window.removeEventListener("pointercancel", up)
    }
    window.addEventListener("pointermove", move)
    window.addEventListener("pointerup", up)
    window.addEventListener("pointercancel", up)
  })

  const floorNote = !here.feasible ? "no sample has this mean" : design.ab ? "with both observed extremes in the sample" : design.alpha !== null && design.quasi ? "raised by the reported α" : design.quasi ? "zero only at whole-number means" : "always zero for continuous data"
  const ceilingNote = design.alpha !== null ? "lowered by the reported α" : design.ab ? "within the observed range" : `at this mean, compared with ${fmt(bd(sxMean))} by the Bhatia–Davis bound`
  const tiles = html`<div class="sb-tiles">
    <div><div class="sb-tile-value" style="color: ${colour};">${fmt(sxSd)}</div><div class="sb-tile-label">Chosen <i>SD</i></div><div class="sb-tile-note">at a mean of ${fmt(sxMean)}</div></div>
    <div><div class="sb-tile-value" style="color: inherit;">${here.feasible ? fmt(here.floor) : "—"}</div><div class="sb-tile-label">Smallest possible <i>SD</i></div><div class="sb-tile-note">${floorNote}</div></div>
    <div><div class="sb-tile-value" style="color: inherit;">${here.feasible ? fmt(here.ceiling) : "—"}</div><div class="sb-tile-label">Largest possible <i>SD</i></div><div class="sb-tile-note">${ceilingNote}</div></div>
    <div><div class="sb-tile-value" style="color: inherit;">${fmt(bd(sxMean) / Math.sqrt(3))}</div><div class="sb-tile-label">Uniform-spread bound</div><div class="sb-tile-note">larger <i>SD</i>s are possible, but need scores piled up at the ends</div></div>
  </div>`
  const legend = html`<div class="bd-legend">
    <span><svg width="28" height="12"><rect width="28" height="12" fill="#2780e3" fill-opacity="0.18"/><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="1" y2="1" stroke="#2780e3" stroke-width="1.5"/></svg> Possible combinations</span>
    ${reference ? html`<span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.35" stroke-dasharray="4,3"/></svg> Bounds from the scale limits alone</span>` : html`<span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.45" stroke-dasharray="6,4"/></svg> Bhatia–Davis bound</span>`}
    <span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.6" stroke-dasharray="1,3" stroke-width="1.5"/></svg> Uniform-spread bound</span>
    ${design.ab ? html`<span><svg width="10" height="12"><line x1="5" x2="5" y1="0" y2="12" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.5" stroke-dasharray="2,3"/></svg> Range of possible means</span>` : ""}
  </div>`
  const feedback = html`<div class="sb-feedback sb-feedback-${verdict.kind}">`
  feedback.innerHTML = verdict.text
  const combined = design.ab && design.alpha !== null ? html`<div class="sc-status">With both a reported α and observed extremes, the bounds are the higher of the two floors and the lower of the two ceilings. These are valid, but may not be as sharp as possible.</div>` : ""
  return html`${abProblem ? html`<div class="sb-feedback sb-feedback-warn">${abProblem}</div>` : ""}${tiles}${plot}${legend}${feedback}${combined}`
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// functions used by the SD bounds explorer. they are the closed-form bounds of the BRIMMER article and the {strait}
// package, for a mean and SD treated as exact. all bounds are calculated on the scale of the sum score, on which
// whole-number items give whole-number scores, and a mean of items is converted to and from it

// the scales of the latest plot, so that a drag that began on an earlier version of it is converted with the current one
sxDrag = ({x: null, y: null})

function sxSet(view, x) {
  // move a range slider to the nearest value it can take, and tell everything that depends on it
  const input = view.querySelector("input[type=range]")
  const min = +input.min, max = +input.max, step = +input.step
  view.value = +Math.min(max, Math.max(min, min + Math.round((x - min) / step) * step)).toFixed(10)
  view.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}))
}

function sxFrac(x) {
  // the fractional part, treating values within rounding error of a whole number as whole
  const f = x - Math.floor(x + 1e-9)
  return f < 1e-9 ? 0 : f
}

function sxCeiling(m, n, l, u) {
  // the largest sample SD with this mean, for n values between l and u: as many values as possible at the two ends,
  // and at most one in between (structure S). this sharpens the Bhatia-Davis bound, which assumes the counts at the
  // ends need not be whole numbers
  const R = u - l, S = n * (m - l)
  const nu = Math.min(Math.floor(S / R + 1e-9), n - 1)
  const xr = l + (S - nu * R), nl = n - nu - 1
  return Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, (nl * (l - m) ** 2 + (xr - m) ** 2 + nu * (u - m) ** 2) / (n - 1)))
}

function sxQuasiFloor(m, n) {
  // the smallest sample SD of n values with this mean when all but one are whole numbers (quasi-integer), which gives
  // a floor at every mean that never rules out anything whole-number data could produce
  const d = sxFrac(m), g = sxFrac(n * m)
  return Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, (n * d * (1 - d) - g * (1 - g)) / (n - 1)))
}

function sxVmaxAlpha(m, k, n, itemL, itemU) {
  // the largest possible sum of the item variances of k whole-number items at sum-score mean m (strait's v_max_alpha)
  const h = (itemU - itemL) / n, T = (m - k * itemL) / h, x = T / k
  const j = Math.min(Math.floor(x + 1e-12), n - 1), th = x - j
  let phi = T - Math.floor(T + 1e-12)
  if (phi > 1 - 1e-9) phi = 0
  const A = jj => h * h * jj * (n - jj)
  return Math.max(0, k * ((1 - th) * A(j) + th * A(j + 1)) - h * h * (n - 1) * phi * (1 - phi))
}

function sxMeanBand(n, a, b) {
  // with one value at the observed minimum and one at the observed maximum, the mean cannot be closer to either end
  // than this
  return [a + (b - a) / n, b - (b - a) / n]
}

function sxBoundsAt(mean, design) {
  // the smallest and largest possible sample SD at this mean, in the units of the score
  const {n, k, quasi, toSum, itemLimits, alpha, ab} = design
  const m = mean * toSum, L = itemLimits[0] * k, U = itemLimits[1] * k
  let floor, ceiling, feasible = true
  if (alpha === null) {
    floor = quasi ? sxQuasiFloor(m, n) : 0
    ceiling = sxCeiling(m, n, L, U)
  } else {
    // a reported alpha caps how much the items can disagree: it lowers the ceiling and amplifies the whole-number
    // floor (strait's sd_bounds_alpha, without its enumeration for strictly integer data)
    const D = 1 - (k - 1) / k * alpha
    ceiling = Math.min(sxCeiling(m, n, L, U), Math.sqrt(n / (n - 1) * Math.max(0, (U - m) * (m - L)) / (k * D)))
    floor = 0
    if (quasi) {
      ceiling = Math.min(ceiling, Math.sqrt(n / (n - 1) * sxVmaxAlpha(m, k, n, itemLimits[0], itemLimits[1]) / D))
      floor = sxQuasiFloor(m, n) / Math.sqrt(D)
    }
  }
  if (ab) {
    // one value at each observed extreme, and the other n - 2 as close together as their mean allows
    const [a, b] = ab.map(x => x * toSum), [lo, hi] = sxMeanBand(n, a, b)
    if (m < lo - 1e-9 || m > hi + 1e-9) return {floor: NaN, ceiling: NaN, feasible: false}
    let abFloor
    if (n === 2) abFloor = (b - a) / Math.SQRT2
    else {
      const p = m - a, q = b - m, kk = n - 2
      let ss = p * p + q * q + (p - q) ** 2 / kk
      if (quasi) {
        const inner = (n * m - a - b) / kk, d = sxFrac(inner), g = sxFrac(n * m)
        ss += Math.max(0, kk * d * (1 - d) - g * (1 - g))
      }
      abFloor = Math.sqrt(ss / (n - 1))
    }
    // with alpha as well, the higher floor and the lower ceiling
    floor = Math.max(alpha === null ? 0 : floor, abFloor)
    ceiling = Math.min(alpha === null ? Infinity : ceiling, sxCeiling(m, n, a, b))
  }
  if (floor > ceiling + 1e-9) feasible = false
  return {floor: floor / toSum, ceiling: ceiling / toSum, feasible}
}

function sxParityMax(l, u, n) {
  // the largest SD any sample of this size can have on this scale, whatever its mean (Popoviciu, with the odd-n case)
  return (u - l) / 2 * Math.sqrt(n / (n - 1) * (2 * n * n - 1 + (-1) ** n) / (2 * n * n))
}

function sxVerdict(m, s, here, design, uniform) {
  const f = x => x.toFixed(2), {n, ab, alpha, quasi} = design
  const given = [ab ? "the observed minimum and maximum" : null, alpha !== null ? `an α of ${f(alpha)}` : null].filter(Boolean).join(" and ")
  if (!here.feasible) {
    if (ab && Number.isNaN(here.floor)) {
      const [lo, hi] = sxMeanBand(n, ...ab)
      return {kind: "bad", text: `<strong>Not possible.</strong> With one value at the observed minimum of ${ab[0]} and one at the observed maximum of ${ab[1]}, the mean of ${n} values must lie between ${f(lo)} and ${f(hi)}, whatever the <em>SD</em>.`}
    }
    return {kind: "bad", text: `<strong>Not possible.</strong> No sample of ${n} values with a mean of ${f(m)} satisfies all of the constraints at once: the smallest <em>SD</em> they allow is larger than the largest.`}
  }
  if (s > here.ceiling + 1e-9) return {kind: "bad", text: `<strong>Not possible.</strong> With a mean of ${f(m)}${given ? ` and ${given}` : ""}, the <em>SD</em> of ${n} values can be at most ${f(here.ceiling)}.`}
  if (s < here.floor - 1e-9) return {kind: "bad", text: `<strong>Not possible.</strong> With a mean of ${f(m)}${given ? ` and ${given}` : ""}, the <em>SD</em> of ${n} ${quasi ? "whole-number " : ""}values must be at least ${f(here.floor)}.`}
  if (s > uniform) return {kind: "warn", text: `<strong>Possible, but unusual.</strong> With a mean of ${f(m)}, the <em>SD</em> of ${n} values can be anywhere from ${f(here.floor)} to ${f(here.ceiling)}, but an <em>SD</em> above ${f(uniform)} is more spread out than scores spread evenly across the whole scale. It requires the scores to pile up at the ends of the scale, which is plausible for some measures but not most.`}
  return {kind: "ok", text: `<strong>Possible.</strong> With a mean of ${f(m)}${given ? ` and ${given}` : ""}, the <em>SD</em> of ${n} ${quasi ? "whole-number " : ""}values can be anywhere from ${f(here.floor)} to ${f(here.ceiling)}.`}
}
```

Start with the mean at 3 on the 1–7 scale and raise the *SD* until the point turns red: the largest possible *SD* is close to the Bhatia–Davis bound, but slightly below it, because the number of people at each end of the scale has to be a whole number. On the way, the point turns amber as it crosses the uniform-spread bound, where the scores would have to pile up at the ends of the scale. Move the mean towards either end and the largest possible *SD* falls. With whole-number responses, the smallest possible *SD* is zero only when the mean is a whole number, and rises to a small peak between whole numbers. Now choose a mean of three items and tick **Cronbach's α**: the higher the α, the lower the ceiling, because items that agree with one another cannot produce scores as spread out as items that disagree. Finally, tick **Observed minimum and maximum**: with scores known to include both the minimum and the maximum given, the band lifts well off the floor, the ceiling falls, and means near the ends of the scale become impossible.

To check values reported in an article, use the app in @sec-combined-app, which combines these bounds with the granularity checks of @sec-granularity and allows for rounding.

## Estimates inside confidence intervals {#sec-estimates-in-cis}

Most estimates in quantitative research are reported with a confidence interval: a mean difference, a regression coefficient, an odds ratio, or a correlation, followed by its lower and upper bounds. The estimate and its interval are calculated from the same data by the same analysis, so they are not free to take any values relative to one another. This gives two checks that need nothing but the three reported numbers. The first is a possibility check: is the estimate inside its interval? The second is a plausibility check: is the estimate in the middle of its interval, as it should be for many common methods, once rounding is taken into account?

### Possibility: is the estimate inside its interval? {#sec-estimate-inside-ci}

For almost every method used in practice, a confidence interval contains its own point estimate. An estimate outside its interval is therefore close to proof that at least one of the three numbers is wrong. The exceptions are rare and exotic, such as percentile bootstrap intervals for heavily biased statistics, and an article that used such a method would be expected to say so. More common explanations are a typo, digits transposed while copying, values copied from the wrong row or the wrong model, or bounds and estimates entered in the wrong order. An estimate that equals one of its bounds is technically inside the interval, but for most methods it is no more plausible than one outside it.

@georgescu2018 automatically extracted 244,750 ratios (odds ratios, risk ratios, and hazard ratios) and their 95% confidence intervals from the abstracts of articles indexed in MEDLINE. Between 0.4% and 0.6% of the ratios, depending on the type, were outside their own intervals. A reanalysis of their data for this book, using the 151,461 ratios whose values could be checked with the rounding of each value taken into account, found that 0.43% were outside their intervals, and that 0.8% of the abstracts contained at least one such ratio. These are small percentages, but they come from abstracts, which usually contain an article's main results, and almost every one of them points to an error, in the article or, occasionally, in the automated extraction.

### Plausibility: is the estimate in the middle of its interval? {#sec-estimate-centred-ci}

Many confidence intervals are symmetric around their estimate. The usual interval for a mean, a mean difference, or a coefficient in a linear regression is the estimate plus or minus a multiple of its standard error, so the estimate lies exactly halfway between the bounds. Intervals for ratios such as odds ratios, risk ratios, and hazard ratios are usually calculated in the same way on the log scale and then exponentiated, so the estimate lies halfway between the bounds on the log scale: it is the geometric mean of the two bounds, √(*lower* × *upper*), rather than their arithmetic mean. This was the basis of the recalculations by @georgescu2018.

Rounding means that the reported estimate need not be exactly in the middle of the reported bounds. Each of the three numbers was rounded separately, so the check asks whether any combination of unrounded values that would round to the three reported numbers places the estimate exactly in the middle. For example, an odds ratio reported as 8.4 [3.7, 19.2] passes: the geometric mean of the bounds is 8.43, which rounds to 8.4. An odds ratio of 1.52 [1.18, 1.93] does not: whatever the unrounded bounds were, their geometric mean lies between 1.504 and 1.514, and no unrounded estimate between 1.515 and 1.525 can equal it. The difference is small, but it is larger than rounding can produce.

Unlike an estimate outside its interval, an estimate that is off-centre is not proof of an error, because many legitimate methods produce intervals that are not symmetric around their estimate on any simple scale. Examples include profile likelihood intervals, which R uses by default for the coefficients of logistic and other generalised linear models; exact intervals, such as Clopper–Pearson intervals for proportions and conditional intervals for odds ratios from small samples; Wilson intervals for proportions; intervals for correlations calculated through Fisher's *z* transformation, which are symmetric on the *z* scale but not on the scale of the correlation; intervals for Standardized Mean Differences based on the noncentral *t* distribution; bootstrap intervals, which can be asymmetric even when the model itself assumes normally distributed errors, because they follow the shape of the bootstrap distribution rather than a formula; and Bayesian credible intervals from skewed posterior distributions. Whether an off-centre estimate is a concern therefore depends on the metric and on the method used to calculate its interval. An off-centre coefficient from an ordinary least squares regression with standard intervals is a strong sign of an error. An off-centre odds ratio from a profile likelihood interval is expected.

In the reanalysis of the data of @georgescu2018, 92.7% of the ratios were centred on the log scale given rounding, 6.8% were inside their intervals but off-centre, and 0.43% were outside their intervals. The histograms below show where each estimate fell, as a proportion of the width of its interval on the log scale: 0% is the lower bound, 50% the middle, and 100% the upper bound. Most off-centre estimates are only slightly off-centre, and many of them are probably the result of legitimate asymmetric methods, which these abstracts rarely describe. About 2.1% of all ratios were both off-centre given rounding and outside the middle fifth of their interval (40% to 60% of its width), which is much harder to explain by method alone.

### Seeing the problem

Problems of this kind are much easier to see in a plot than in a table. Reading down a column of numbers such as −0.05 [−0.50, −0.11], it is easy to miss that the estimate is not between its bounds, and almost impossible to judge by eye whether an estimate is in the middle of its interval. Plotted, an estimate outside its interval, or one that sits far from the middle of it, stands out immediately.

@haller2022 reported a multiple regression predicting prosocial behaviour from demographic and psychological variables, with standardised coefficients and 95% confidence intervals in their Table 5. As a comment on [PubPeer](https://pubpeer.com/publications/480E5B0C4CA6A1B2C3EE84841140BB) pointed out, the coefficient for being divorced, *β* = −0.05, is outside its interval of [−0.50, −0.11], which is not possible. The article describes an ordinary multiple regression, for which symmetric intervals are expected, but the coefficient for being widowed, *β* = −0.29 [−0.34, −0.01], is far from the middle of its interval, and the coefficient for high perceived stress, *β* = 0.29 [0.29, 0.04], equals one of its bounds, which are also in the wrong order. A coefficient reported in the text, *β* = 0.15 [0.12, 0.22] for Western Europe, which the same comment quoted for a different reason, is also off-centre. Each of these is easy to miss in the table. Load the table into the app below with the **Haller et al. (2022), Table 5** button to see how they look in a plot. The **Odds ratios from MEDLINE abstracts** button loads seven odds ratios from the abstracts analysed by @georgescu2018, as extracted, to be checked on the log scale.

The app below plots any number of estimates and their intervals. Enter a label, the estimate, and the lower and upper bounds in each row, or paste a block of cells from a spreadsheet into the cell where the block should start. **Enter the values exactly as reported, including trailing zeros.** The number of decimal places in each value determines how much rounding is allowed for, and so how wide the region that counts as the middle of the interval is: a bound reported as 0.30 could have been anything from 0.295 to 0.305, but one entered as 0.3 could have been anything from 0.25 to 0.35. Spreadsheets often drop trailing zeros, so if you paste values from one, check that they still have the decimal places they were reported with. Choose whether the intervals should be symmetric on the original scale, as for means, mean differences, and regression coefficients, or on the log scale, as for odds ratios, risk ratios, and hazard ratios. Each estimate is coloured green if it is in the middle of its interval given rounding, orange if it is inside its interval but not in the middle, and red if it is outside its interval. The grey band on each interval shows the range of values that would be in the middle of the interval, given rounding. The **Standardise interval widths** button rescales every interval to run from 0% (the lower bound) to 100% (the upper bound), on the scale on which it should be symmetric, and marks the middle at 50%. Each estimate is then shown at its position within its own interval, and the grey band shows the region around 50% that counts as the middle, given rounding. The short coloured bar around each estimate shows the values it could have had before it was rounded, and an estimate counts as in the middle if this bar touches the grey band. This makes intervals of very different widths easy to compare, and shows how much the rounding of the reported values matters: values reported with fewer decimal places, relative to the width of their interval, have a wider band. Clicking the button again shows the reported values.

Some statistical software prints the lower bound before the estimate, as in "lower, estimate, upper", and a value copied from such output into the wrong column can produce an estimate outside its interval. The **Swap estimates and lower bounds** button swaps the two columns in every row, so that you can see whether the values make sense when read in the other order. Clicking it again swaps them back.

```{ojs}
      ["In a relationship", "-0.07", "-0.13", "-0.01"], ["Single", "0.00", "-0.07", "0.07"], ["Divorced", "-0.05", "-0.50", "-0.11"], ["Widowed", "-0.29", "-0.34", "-0.01"],

      ["Moderate social support", "0.34", "0.30", "0.40"], ["High social support", "0.65", "0.59", "0.70"],
      ["Moderate stress", "0.07", "0.02", "0.11"], ["High stress", "0.29", "0.29", "0.04"],
      ["Psychological flexibility", "0.10", "0.07", "0.12"], ["Positive affect", "0.25", "0.23", "0.27"]
    ]},
    "Odds ratios from MEDLINE abstracts": {scale: "log", rows: [
      ["PMID 23118894", "8.4", "3.7", "19.2"], ["PMID 11876688", "5.8", "3.4", "9.7"], ["PMID 17987372", "1.52", "1.18", "1.93"],
      ["PMID 20445803", "2.83", "2.34", "2.91"], ["PMID 26813550", "1.7", "1.6", "2.64"], ["PMID 23870294", "1.12", "1.02", "1.11"], ["PMID 21930284", "1.28", "1.48", "2.99"]
    ]}
  }
  const body = html`<tbody></tbody>`
  const changed = () => view.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}))
  const addRow = (values = []) => {
    const tr = html`<tr></tr>`
    tr.inputs = fields.map(([key, label], j) => {
      const input = html`<input type="text" class="form-control form-control-sm" inputmode="${j === 0 ? "text" : "decimal"}" aria-label="${label}">`
      input.value = values[j] ?? ""
      input.onpaste = e => paste(e, tr, j)
      return input
    })
    const remove = html`<button class="btn btn-sm ci-remove" title="Remove this row" aria-label="Remove this row">×</button>`
    remove.onclick = () => { tr.remove(); if (body.children.length === 0) addRow(); changed() }
    tr.append(...tr.inputs.map(input => html`<td>${input}</td>`), html`<td>${remove}</td>`)
    body.append(tr)
    return tr
  }
  // a block of cells copied from a spreadsheet (tab-separated) or typed as comma-separated values fills the grid
  // from the cell it was pasted into, adding rows as needed. a single value is pasted as normal
  const paste = (e, tr, j) => {
    const text = e.clipboardData.getData("text").replace(/\r/g, "").replace(/\n+$/, "")
    if (!/[\t\n,]/.test(text)) return
    e.preventDefault()
    let row = tr
    for (const line of text.split("\n")) {
      const cells = line.split(line.includes("\t") ? "\t" : ",")
      cells.forEach((cell, k) => { if (j + k < fields.length) row.inputs[j + k].value = cell.trim() })
      row = row.nextElementSibling ?? addRow()
    }
    if (row !== tr && row.inputs.every(input => input.value === "") && row.previousElementSibling) row.remove()
    changed()
  }
  const scale = html`<select class="form-select form-select-sm" aria-label="Scale on which the intervals are symmetric">
    <option value="linear">Symmetric on the original scale (e.g., means, mean differences, regression coefficients)</option>
    <option value="log">Symmetric on the log scale (e.g., odds ratios, risk ratios, hazard ratios)</option>
  </select>`
  // the plot shows either the reported values or every interval rescaled to run from 0% to 100%
  let display = "absolute"
  const standardise = html`<button class="btn btn-quarto">Standardise interval widths (0–100%)</button>`
  standardise.onclick = () => {
    display = display === "absolute" ? "relative" : "absolute"
    standardise.textContent = display === "absolute" ? "Standardise interval widths (0–100%)" : "Show the reported values"
    changed()
  }
  const load = ({scale: s, rows}) => { body.replaceChildren(); rows.forEach(values => addRow(values)); scale.value = s; changed() }
  const exampleButtons = Object.entries(examples).map(([name, example]) => {
    const button = html`<button class="btn btn-quarto">${name}</button>`
    button.onclick = () => load(example)
    return button
  })
  const add = html`<button class="btn btn-quarto">Add row</button>`
  const clear = html`<button class="btn btn-quarto">Clear all</button>`
  const swap = html`<button class="btn btn-quarto">Swap estimates and lower bounds</button>`
  add.onclick = () => addRow().inputs[0].focus()
  clear.onclick = () => { body.replaceChildren(); addRow().inputs[0].focus(); changed() }
  swap.onclick = () => {
    for (const tr of body.children) [tr.inputs[1].value, tr.inputs[2].value] = [tr.inputs[2].value, tr.inputs[1].value]
    changed()
  }
  const view = html`<div>
    <div class="sb-buttons ci-examples"><span>Examples:</span>${exampleButtons}</div>
    <div class="table-responsive"><table class="table table-sm ci-grid">
      <thead><tr><th>Label</th><th>Estimate</th><th>Lower bound</th><th>Upper bound</th><th></th></tr></thead>
      ${body}
    </table></div>
    <div class="sb-buttons">${add}${clear}${swap}</div>
    <div class="ci-controls"><label class="ci-label">Intervals are expected to be</label>${scale}</div>
    <div class="sb-buttons">${standardise}</div>
  </div>`
  // the value is read from the grid whenever anything in it changes, so that the plot follows the typing
  const read = () => ({
    rows: [...body.children].map(tr => Object.fromEntries(fields.map(([key], j) => [key, tr.inputs[j].value.trim()]))),
    scale: scale.value, display
  })
  view.addEventListener("input", () => { view.value = read() }, {capture: true})
  scale.addEventListener("change", changed)
  load(examples["Haller et al. (2022), Table 5"])
  view.value = read()
  return view
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const log = ciInput.scale === "log", relative = ciInput.display === "relative"
  const rows = ciChecked(ciInput.rows, log)
  const valid = rows.filter(r => r.valid)
  const problems = rows.filter(r => !r.valid)
  const problemNote = problems.length ? html`<div class="sc-status">Not plotted: ${problems.map(r => `${r.label} (${r.problem.toLowerCase()})`).join("; ")}.</div>` : ""
  if (valid.length === 0) return html`<div class="sc-status">Enter an estimate and both bounds in at least one row.</div>${problemNote}`

  // in the relative view, every interval runs from 0 to 1 on the scale on which it should be symmetric. positions far
  // outside the interval are drawn at the edge of the plot, so that no estimate disappears
  const clamp = x => Math.max(-0.5, Math.min(1.5, x))
  const pos = relative
    ? valid.map(r => ({...r, xEst: clamp(r.rel), xLow: 0, xUp: 1, xMin: clamp(r.relMin), xMax: clamp(r.relMax), xEstLow: clamp(r.relEstLow), xEstHigh: clamp(r.relEstHigh)}))
    : valid.map(r => ({...r, xEst: r.est, xLow: r.lo, xUp: r.hi, xMin: r.impliedMin, xMax: r.impliedMax, xEstLow: r.estLow, xEstHigh: r.estHigh}))
  const texts = pos.map(r => `${r.label}   ${r.estimateText} [${r.lowerText}, ${r.upperText}]`)
  const marginLeft = Math.min(Math.round(width * 0.5), 16 + 6.6 * d3.max(texts, t => t.length))
  const extent = d3.extent(pos.flatMap(r => [r.xEst, r.xLow, r.xUp, r.xMin, r.xMax]))
  const reference = relative ? 0.5 : log ? 1 : 0
  // the standardised view always shows -10% to 110%, and stretches to show estimates further outside their intervals
  const xDomain = relative ? [Math.min(-0.1, extent[0] - 0.05), Math.max(1.1, extent[1] + 0.05)] : extent
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width, height: 60 + 26 * pos.length, marginLeft, marginRight: 24, marginTop: 10, marginBottom: 45,
    x: relative
      ? {label: `Position within the interval${log ? " on the log scale" : ""} (0% = lower bound, 100% = upper bound)`, labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36, domain: xDomain, ticks: d3.range(-0.5, 1.51, 0.25).filter(t => t >= xDomain[0] && t <= xDomain[1]), tickFormat: d3.format(".0%")}
      : {label: log ? "Estimate (log scale)" : "Estimate", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36, type: log ? "log" : "linear", domain: xDomain, nice: true},
    y: {domain: d3.range(pos.length), tickFormat: i => texts[i], label: null, padding: 0.55, tickSize: 0},
    style: {fontSize: "12px"},
    marks: [
      relative ? Plot.rect([{x1: xDomain[0], x2: 0}, {x1: 1, x2: xDomain[1]}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.06}) : null,
      (relative || (reference >= extent[0] && reference <= extent[1])) ? Plot.ruleX([reference], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.35, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}) : null,
      // the range of values that would be in the middle of the interval, given rounding
      Plot.ruleY(pos.map((r, i) => ({...r, i})), {y: "i", x1: "xMin", x2: "xMax", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.2, strokeWidth: 10}),
      // the interval, with a tick at each end
      Plot.ruleY(pos.map((r, i) => ({...r, i})), {y: "i", x1: "xLow", x2: "xUp", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      Plot.tickX(pos.map((r, i) => ({...r, i})), {y: "i", x: "xLow", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      Plot.tickX(pos.map((r, i) => ({...r, i})), {y: "i", x: "xUp", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      // in the standardised view, the middle of each interval is marked
      relative ? Plot.tickX(pos.map((r, i) => ({...r, i})), {y: "i", x: 0.5, stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 2.5}) : null,
      // the values the estimate could have had before rounding. an estimate counts as in the middle if this bar touches
      // the grey band
      Plot.ruleY(pos.map((r, i) => ({...r, i})), {y: "i", x1: "xEstLow", x2: "xEstHigh", stroke: r => ciColours[r.status], strokeWidth: 4, strokeOpacity: 0.7}),
      Plot.dot(pos.map((r, i) => ({...r, i})), {y: "i", x: "xEst", r: 5.5, fill: r => ciColours[r.status], stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 1, title: r => `${r.label}: ${ciStatusText[r.status]}`})
    ]
  })
  const legend = html`<div class="bd-legend ci-legend">
    ${["centred", "offcentre", "outside"].map(s => html`<span><svg width="12" height="12"><circle cx="6" cy="6" r="5" fill="${ciColours[s]}"/></svg> ${ciStatusText[s]}</span>`)}
    ${relative ? html`<span><svg width="6" height="12"><line x1="3" x2="3" y1="0" y2="12" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5"/></svg> Middle of the interval (50%)</span>` : ""}
    <span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="10" stroke-opacity="0.2"/></svg> ${relative ? "Region that counts as the middle, given rounding" : "Values in the middle of the interval, given rounding"}</span>
    <span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4" stroke-opacity="0.7"/></svg> Values the estimate could have had before rounding</span>
  </div>`

  const named = list => list.map(r => r.label).join(", ")
  const outside = valid.filter(r => r.status === "outside"), off = valid.filter(r => r.status === "offcentre"), reversed = valid.filter(r => r.reversed)
  const parts = []
  if (outside.length) parts.push(`<strong>${outside.length} of ${valid.length} estimates ${outside.length === 1 ? "is" : "are"} outside ${outside.length === 1 ? "its interval" : "their intervals"}</strong>, which is not possible for almost any method: ${named(outside)}.`)
  if (off.length) parts.push(`<strong>${off.length} ${off.length === 1 ? "estimate is" : "estimates are"} inside ${off.length === 1 ? "its interval" : "their intervals"} but not in the middle</strong>, given rounding: ${named(off)}. This is unexpected if the intervals were calculated as the estimate plus or minus a multiple of its standard error${log ? " on the log scale" : ""}, but expected for some other methods.`)
  if (reversed.length) parts.push(`The lower bound is above the upper bound in ${named(reversed)}. These intervals were checked with their bounds in the correct order.`)
  if (!outside.length && !off.length) parts.push(`<strong>All ${valid.length} ${valid.length === 1 ? "estimate is" : "estimates are"} in the middle of ${valid.length === 1 ? "its interval" : "their intervals"}</strong>, given rounding${log ? " on the log scale" : ""}.`)
  const feedback = html`<div class="sb-feedback sb-feedback-${outside.length ? "bad" : off.length || reversed.length ? "warn" : "ok"}">`
  feedback.innerHTML = parts.join(" ")
  return html`${plot}${legend}${feedback}${problemNote}`
}
```
