```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// functions and styles used by the estimates in confidence intervals plots

ciColours = ({centred: "#3b9c6e", offcentre: "#e08a1e", outside: "#c0392b"})
ciStatusText = ({centred: "In the middle of the interval, given rounding", offcentre: "Inside the interval, but not in the middle", outside: "Outside the interval"})

function ciChecked(rows, log) {
  // checks each row of the grid. rows that are entirely empty are left out. the number of decimal places of each value
  // is read from the text as entered, so trailing zeros count. each value could have been anything that rounds to it,
  // so the estimate is in the middle of its interval if any combination of unrounded values puts it exactly in the
  // middle: the range of possible estimates must overlap the range of possible midpoints of the bounds. on the log
  // scale, the midpoint is the geometric mean of the bounds
  const number = s => s === "" ? NaN : Number(s.replace(/[−–]/g, "-"))
  const decimals = s => (s.match(/\.(\d+)/)?.[1].length) ?? 0
  return rows.map((r, i) => ({...r, label: r.label || `Row ${i + 1}`}))
    .filter(r => r.estimate !== "" || r.lower !== "" || r.upper !== "")
    .map(r => {
      const est = number(r.estimate), lower = number(r.lower), upper = number(r.upper)
      const base = {label: r.label, estimateText: r.estimate, lowerText: r.lower, upperText: r.upper}
      if (![est, lower, upper].every(Number.isFinite)) return {...base, valid: false, problem: "Missing or non-numeric values"}
      if (log && [est, lower, upper].some(x => x <= 0)) return {...base, valid: false, problem: "Values must be above zero on the log scale"}
      const reversed = lower > upper
      const [lo, hi] = reversed ? [upper, lower] : [lower, upper]
      const [loText, hiText] = reversed ? [r.upper, r.lower] : [r.lower, r.upper]
      const half = s => 0.5 * 10 ** -decimals(s)
      // values on the scale on which the interval should be symmetric. a rounded bound of zero is kept just above zero
      const f = log ? x => Math.log(Math.max(x, 1e-12)) : x => x
      const inv = log ? Math.exp : x => x
      const midMin = (f(lo - half(loText)) + f(hi - half(hiText))) / 2, midMax = (f(lo + half(loText)) + f(hi + half(hiText))) / 2
      const estMin = f(est - half(r.estimate)), estMax = f(est + half(r.estimate))
      const centred = Math.max(midMin, estMin) <= Math.min(midMax, estMax) + 1e-12
      const inside = lo <= est && est <= hi
      const span = f(hi) - f(lo)
      // an interval of zero width has no position within it; its estimate is drawn in the middle
      const rel = span > 0 ? (f(est) - f(lo)) / span : 0.5
      return {...base, valid: true, est, lo, hi, reversed,
        status: !inside ? "outside" : !centred ? "offcentre" : "centred",
        impliedMin: inv(midMin), impliedMax: inv(midMax), rel,
        relMin: span > 0 ? (midMin - f(lo)) / span : 0.5, relMax: span > 0 ? (midMax - f(lo)) / span : 0.5,
        // the values the estimate could have had before it was rounded
        estLow: inv(estMin), estHigh: inv(estMax),
        relEstLow: span > 0 ? (estMin - f(lo)) / span : 0.5, relEstHigh: span > 0 ? (estMax - f(lo)) / span : 0.5}
    })
}

ciStyle = html`<style>
  .sb-buttons { display: flex; gap: 0.5rem; flex-wrap: wrap; align-items: center; }
  .sc-status { margin: 0.5rem 0 1.5rem; color: var(--bs-secondary-color); font-size: 0.9rem; }
  .ci-examples { margin: 0.5rem 0 0.75rem; font-size: 0.9rem; }
  .ci-grid { font-size: 0.9rem; margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }
  .ci-grid th { text-align: center; font-weight: 600; border-bottom-width: 1px; }
  .ci-grid td { padding: 0.15rem; }
  .ci-grid input { min-width: 4rem; text-align: right; background: transparent; color: inherit; }
  .ci-grid td:first-child input { min-width: 10rem; text-align: left; }
  .ci-remove { line-height: 1; padding: 0.2rem 0.5rem; color: var(--bs-secondary-color); }
  .ci-controls { margin: 0.75rem 0; max-width: 34rem; }
  .ci-label { font-weight: 600; display: block; margin: 0.5rem 0 0.25rem; }
  .bd-legend { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.25rem 1.25rem; justify-content: center; font-size: 0.8rem; margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }
  .bd-legend svg { vertical-align: middle; }
  .ci-hist-title { font-size: 0.9rem; font-weight: 600; border-left: 4px solid; padding-left: 0.5rem; margin-top: 0.75rem; }
  .ci-hists { margin-bottom: 1.5rem; }
</style>`
```

Swapping the columns does not let the authors off the hook, even when it makes every estimate sit neatly in the middle of its interval. Readers, reviewers, and meta-analysts usually take reported numbers at face value. A meta-analyst who extracts the estimate and calculates its standard error from the width of the interval, as is common, will use the wrong estimate, the wrong standard error, or both, and nothing in the meta-analysis will reveal the error. An error that would be obvious in a plot of one study can therefore distort the pooled results of many.

## Coefficient bounds {#sec-coefficient-bounds}

Many coefficients have bounds that follow from how they are defined, whatever was measured. A correlation must lie between −1 and 1, and a proportion or an *R*^2^ between 0 and 1. Reliability, defined as the proportion of the variance in scores that is true-score variance, also lies between 0 and 1, but the coefficients used to estimate it are bounded less tightly. Cronbach's α cannot exceed 1, but it has no lower bound: it is negative whenever the items are, on average, negatively correlated with one another, as happens when reverse-keyed items have not been reverse-scored, and two items that correlate −.90 give an α of −18. A negative α is therefore possible, but it shows that the items do not measure one thing in the way they were scored, and so it is a reason to look closely. A reported value outside a coefficient's bounds cannot be correct. @tbl-coefficient-bounds lists the bounds of some statistics that are common in psychology and medicine.

| Statistic | Bounds | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Pearson's *r*, Spearman's *ρ*, Kendall's *τ*, point-biserial and phi correlations | −1 to 1 | For phi and point-biserial correlations, the attainable maximum is often smaller, depending on the proportions in each category. |
| Proportions, probabilities, and *p*-values | 0 to 1 (0% to 100%) | Includes prevalence, response rates, and proportions of variance. |
| Sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score | 0 to 1 | All are proportions, and the F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it lies between them. |
| Area under the ROC curve (AUC, *c*-statistic) | 0 to 1 | 0.5 is chance. Values below 0.5 mean that the predictor works in the opposite direction to the one assumed. |
| *R*^2^, *η*^2^, partial *η*^2^, Cramér's *V* | 0 to 1 | |
| Adjusted *R*^2^ | −*p* / (*n* − *p* − 1) to 1, with *p* predictors | Can be slightly negative when *R*^2^ is close to zero: at least −0.03 with 3 predictors and 100 people. It is only substantially negative when there are many predictors for the sample size. |
| *ω*^2^ (one-way ANOVA) | −*df*~effect~ / (*N* − *df*~effect~) to 1 | Can be slightly negative when the effect is close to zero: at least −0.01 for two groups and 100 people. Often reported as 0 when negative. |
| *ε*^2^ (one-way ANOVA) | −*df*~effect~ / *df*~error~ to 1 | As for *ω*^2^: at least −0.01 for two groups of 50. |
| Standardised regression coefficients (*β*) | −1 to 1 with one predictor | With several correlated predictors, values beyond ±1 are possible, but rare, and worth a closer look. |
| Standardised factor loadings | −1 to 1 | A value beyond ±1, known as a Heywood case, indicates an improper solution. |
| Cronbach's *α* | Up to 1, with no lower bound | Negative when the items are on average negatively correlated, usually because reverse-keyed items were not reverse-scored. A slightly negative *α* is possible but a sign of a problem with the scale or its scoring. A value far below 0, such as −5, needs items that are strongly negatively correlated, which is implausible for a published scale unless the article explains it. |
| McDonald's *ω* | 0 to 1 | |
| Single-measure intraclass correlation (one-way, or two-way consistency) | −1 / (*k* − 1) to 1, with *k* raters or measurements per subject | −1 to 1 with two raters, and closer to 0 with more. Estimates are negative when the variance between subjects is close to zero, and are then usually only slightly negative. The two-way agreement form can fall slightly further below in very small samples. |
| Average-measure intraclass correlation | Up to 1, with no lower bound | The consistency form is identical to Cronbach's *α*, and is negative under the same circumstances. |
| Cohen's *κ* | −1 to 1 | The attainable maximum is often below 1, depending on the marginal proportions. |
| Odds ratio, risk ratio, hazard ratio | Above 0 | 1 means no difference. Ratios cannot be zero or negative, so neither can the bounds of their intervals, although a small lower bound can be rounded to 0.00. |
| Risk difference | −1 to 1 | |
| Number needed to treat (NNT) | 1 or more in size | An NNT between −1 and 1 would imply a risk difference greater than 1 in size. |
| Variances, *SD*s, and standard errors | 0 or more | For a single mean, the standard error, *SD* / √*N*, cannot be larger than the *SD*. |
| *I*^2^ | 0% to 100% | |
| *τ*^2^, *χ*^2^, *F*, RMSEA, SRMR | 0 or more | |
| CFI | 0 to 1 | The TLI is not bounded in the same way, and can fall below 0 or rise above 1. |
| Cohen's *d* and other Standardized Mean Differences | No bounds by definition | On a bounded scale, the bounds of the scale limit how large a Standardized Mean Difference can be (@sec-bounded-data). |

: Bounds of some common statistics. {#tbl-coefficient-bounds}

Some of the statistics in @tbl-coefficient-bounds are bias-corrected or variance-based estimates that can legitimately fall slightly below zero when the quantity they estimate is close to zero, such as adjusted *R*^2^, *ω*^2^, and the intraclass correlation. Being able to fall slightly below zero does not mean that they have no bounds. Most of them have a lower bound that follows from the sample size or design, and it is usually close to zero. An *R*^2^ of −4.1 is impossible, because *R*^2^ cannot be negative at all, and an adjusted *R*^2^ that negative would need an *R*^2^ of zero and almost as many predictors as people. A single-measure intraclass correlation of −9.1 is also impossible in practice: the one-way and consistency forms cannot fall below −1 with any number of raters, and the agreement form can only do so in samples of a few subjects. Only a few statistics, such as Cronbach's *α* and the average-measure intraclass correlation, have no lower bound at all, and even for these, a value far below zero is implausible without a specific explanation.

Values this obviously wrong still reach print. @hussein2022 compared machine learning models for classifying lung diseases from chest X-rays, and reported each model's accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall), so it must lie between them, and like them between 0 and 1. As a comment on [PubPeer](https://pubpeer.com/publications/7B4601B575EDFC92F0864708986D78) pointed out, every F1 score in the article's Tables 2 to 4 is above 1, ranging from 1.40 to 3.64. They are not percentages, because the precision and recall in the same rows are reported as proportions. Almost all of them are four times the recall in the same row: one model was reported with a precision of .6900, a recall of .6891, and an F1 score of 2.7563, whereas the F1 score implied by its precision and recall is .6895. Whatever the cause, none of the F1 scores can be correct. Later comments on the same article raise further questions about the other metrics in these tables.

Values that only break a bound once they are combined with other reported numbers are probably more common, because no one checks the combination. The next section describes one such check.

### Disattenuated correlations {#sec-disattenuation}

Measurement error weakens correlations. If two measures are not perfectly reliable, the correlation between them is smaller in size than the correlation between the constructs they measure, a bias known as attenuation. @spearman1904 showed how to correct for it: divide the observed correlation by the square root of the product of the two measures' reliabilities,

$$
r_{xy}^{\text{true}} = \frac{r_{xy}}{\sqrt{r_{xx} \, r_{yy}}},
$$

where *r*~*xy*~ is the observed correlation and *r*~*xx*~ and *r*~*yy*~ are the reliabilities of the two measures, such as Cronbach's α or a test–retest correlation. The disattenuated correlation is an estimate of the correlation between the constructs, and like any correlation it must lie between −1 and 1.

This gives a check that uses three numbers which articles often report together. Rearranging the formula, a correlation can only be as large as the square root of the product of the reliabilities: two measures with reliabilities of .70 can correlate at most .70, however closely related the constructs are. A reported correlation of .80 between them implies a disattenuated correlation of 1.14, which is impossible. Either the correlation, at least one of the reliabilities, or both are wrong, or the reliabilities were estimated in a different sample from the correlation.

Whether a disattenuated correlation outside −1 to 1 shows that the reported numbers are impossible, or only that they are implausible, depends on where the reliabilities come from. When the correlation and both reliabilities were estimated in the same sample, as when an article reports all three, they describe the same data, and the check is a possibility check: the numbers cannot all be correct, subject to the caveats about sampling error and the type of reliability below. When the reliabilities come from other samples, such as a test manual, earlier studies, or a meta-analysis, the check is a plausibility check. The reliabilities then describe what is typical for the measures, and the measures may have been more or less reliable in the sample at hand, so a disattenuated correlation outside −1 to 1 shows that the reported correlation is implausible given what is known about the measures, not that it is impossible. For the same reason, √(*r*~*xx*~ *r*~*yy*~) is a ceiling on the correlation to be expected between two measures, not on the correlation that can be observed in any one sample, which varies around its expected value.

The plausibility check can be applied to meta-analyses as well as to single studies. @vahey2015 reported a meta-analytic correlation of *r* = .45 between the Implicit Relational Assessment Procedure (IRAP), a reaction-time-based measure, and clinical criterion measures. A later meta-analysis estimated the IRAP's internal consistency at α = .27 and its test–retest reliability at .18 [@husseydrake2020]. As @hussey2025irap pointed out, these estimates are incompatible with one another. Even if the criterion measures were assumed to be highly reliable (*r*~*yy*~ = .90), the disattenuated correlation would be .91 using the IRAP's internal consistency and 1.12 using its test–retest reliability. With a lower and arguably more plausible criterion reliability of .70, it would be 1.04 or 1.27. Either the meta-analytic correlation was too large, or the meta-analytic reliabilities were too small. A reanalysis of the original meta-analysis found serious errors that generally inflated the effect size, and a new meta-analysis calculated to show their combined impact produced an estimate half the size, *r* = .22 [@hussey2025irap].

Enter a reported correlation and the reliabilities of the two measures below, and choose whether the reliabilities come from the same sample as the correlation, which makes the check a possibility check, or from other samples, which makes it a plausibility check. The plot shows the reported correlation and the disattenuated correlation, joined by an arrow; the grey areas outside −1 and 1 are impossible for any correlation. You can also click or drag anywhere on the plot to set the reported correlation. The app uses the values exactly as entered and does not allow for their rounding, so it is better treated as an intuition pump than as a formal test.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof dcR = Inputs.number([-1, 1], {value: 0.20, step: 0.01, label: "Correlation (r_xy)"})
// reliability estimates such as alpha can be negative, so the reliability boxes accept any value up to 1
viewof dcRxx = Inputs.number([-Infinity, 1], {value: 0.70, step: 0.01, label: "Reliability of measure 1 (r_xx)"})
viewof dcRyy = Inputs.number([-Infinity, 1], {value: 0.70, step: 0.01, label: "Reliability of measure 2 (r_yy)"})
// reliabilities from the same sample as the correlation make the check a possibility check; reliabilities from other
// samples make it a plausibility check
viewof dcSameSample = Inputs.radio(new Map([["The same sample as the correlation (possibility check)", true], ["Other samples, such as a test manual or meta-analysis (plausibility check)", false]]), {value: true, label: "Reliabilities from"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
dcState = {
  // the inputs, checked: the correlation must be a number in [-1, 1], and the reliabilities numbers no greater than 1.
  // a reliability estimate of zero or below is possible for a coefficient such as alpha, but the correction cannot
  // be applied to it, because it takes the square root of the product of the reliabilities
  const r = dcR, rxx = dcRxx, ryy = dcRyy
  const finite = [r, rxx, ryy].every(Number.isFinite)
  if (!finite) return {error: "Enter the correlation and both reliabilities as numbers."}
  if (r < -1 || r > 1) return {error: "<strong>Not possible.</strong> The reported correlation is itself outside −1 to 1, so it cannot be correct whatever the reliabilities."}
  if (rxx > 1 || ryy > 1) return {error: "<strong>Not possible.</strong> No reliability coefficient can be greater than 1."}
  if (rxx <= 0 || ryy <= 0) return {error: `<strong>Cannot be corrected.</strong> A reliability of ${Math.min(rxx, ryy).toFixed(2).replace("-", "−")} is possible for an estimate such as Cronbach's α, but the correction for attenuation is only defined for reliabilities above 0. A reliability estimate at or below 0 means that the items do not hang together as scored, for example because reverse-keyed items were not reverse-scored, and is itself worth questioning.`, kind: "warn"}
  const ceiling = Math.sqrt(rxx * ryy)
  const dis = r / ceiling
  return {r, rxx, ryy, ceiling, dis, possible: Math.abs(dis) <= 1}
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  if (dcState.error) {
    const box = html`<div class="sb-feedback sb-feedback-${dcState.kind ?? "bad"}">`
    box.innerHTML = dcState.error
    return box
  }
  const {r, rxx, ryy, ceiling, dis, possible} = dcState
  const same = dcSameSample
  const blue = "#2780e3", green = "#3b9c6e", red = "#c0392b", amber = "#d9a02b"
  // outside -1 to 1 is impossible when the reliabilities come from the same sample, and implausible when they do not
  const disColour = possible ? green : same ? red : amber
  const fmt = x => x.toFixed(2).replace("-", "−")

  const tiles = html`<div class="sb-tiles">
    <div><div class="sb-tile-value" style="color: ${blue};">${fmt(r)}</div><div class="sb-tile-label">Reported <i>r</i></div><div class="sb-tile-note">the observed correlation</div></div>
    <div><div class="sb-tile-value" style="color: ${disColour};">${fmt(dis)}</div><div class="sb-tile-label">Disattenuated <i>r</i></div><div class="sb-tile-note">must lie between −1 and 1</div></div>
    <div><div class="sb-tile-value" style="color: inherit;">±${ceiling.toFixed(2)}</div><div class="sb-tile-label">Reliability ceiling on <i>r</i></div><div class="sb-tile-note">√(<i>r<sub>xx</sub></i> × <i>r<sub>yy</sub></i>): the largest correlation to expect with these reliabilities, not a limit on what any one sample can show</div></div>
  </div>`

  // the axis always shows -1 to 1, and stretches to show a disattenuated correlation beyond them
  const span = Math.max(1.25, Math.abs(dis) * 1.12)
  const points = [
    {x: r, label: "reported", colour: blue},
    {x: dis, label: "disattenuated", colour: disColour}
  ]
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width, height: 190, marginLeft: 20, marginRight: 20, marginTop: 10, marginBottom: 40,
    x: {label: "Correlation", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 34, domain: [-span, span], ticks: d3.ticks(-span, span, 10)},
    y: {axis: null, domain: [0, 1]},
    style: {fontSize: "13px"},
    marks: [
      // outside -1 to 1: impossible for any correlation
      Plot.rect([{x1: -span, x2: -1}, {x1: 1, x2: span}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: 0, y2: 1, fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.08}),
      Plot.ruleX([-1, 1], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeOpacity: 0.7}),
      Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.3}),
      // the labels of the grey areas sit at the bottom, below the disattenuated correlation's labels, which can be
      // inside them
      Plot.text(["Impossible"], {x: 1 + (span - 1) / 2, y: 0.03, fontWeight: 600, fillOpacity: 0.6, lineAnchor: "bottom"}),
      Plot.text(["Impossible"], {x: -1 - (span - 1) / 2, y: 0.03, fontWeight: 600, fillOpacity: 0.6, lineAnchor: "bottom"}),
      Math.abs(dis - r) > 1e-9 ? Plot.arrow([{}], {x1: r, x2: dis, y1: 0.5, y2: 0.5, stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.6, strokeWidth: 1.5, insetEnd: 8, headLength: 10}) : null,
      Plot.dot(points, {x: "x", y: 0.5, r: 7, fill: "colour", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      // the reported correlation is labelled below its point and the disattenuated correlation above, so that the
      // labels do not overlap when the two are close together
      Plot.text([points[0]], {x: "x", y: 0.5, text: d => fmt(d.x), dy: 17, fill: "colour", fontWeight: 700}),
      Plot.text([points[0]], {x: "x", y: 0.5, text: "label", dy: 32, fill: "colour"}),
      Plot.text([points[1]], {x: "x", y: 0.5, text: d => fmt(d.x), dy: -16, fill: "colour", fontWeight: 700}),
      Plot.text([points[1]], {x: "x", y: 0.5, text: "label", dy: -31, fill: "colour"})
    ]
  })
  // clicking the plot sets the reported correlation to the clicked value, and dragging moves it continuously. the
  // plot is redrawn at every change, and its axis can stretch as the disattenuated correlation grows, so the drag is
  // followed on the window and positions are converted with the latest plot's scale
  dcDrag.scale = plot.scale("x")
  plot.style.cursor = "crosshair"
  plot.style.touchAction = "none"
  plot.addEventListener("pointerdown", down => {
    const box = plot.getBoundingClientRect()
    const setR = event => {
      const value = dcDrag.scale.invert((event.clientX - box.left) * width / box.width)
      viewof dcR.value = Math.max(-1, Math.min(1, Math.round(value * 100) / 100))
      viewof dcR.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}))
    }
    down.preventDefault()
    setR(down)
    let pending = null
    const move = event => {
      if (pending === null) requestAnimationFrame(() => { setR(pending); pending = null })
      pending = event
    }
    const up = () => {
      window.removeEventListener("pointermove", move)
      window.removeEventListener("pointerup", up)
      window.removeEventListener("pointercancel", up)
    }
    window.addEventListener("pointermove", move)
    window.addEventListener("pointerup", up)
    window.addEventListener("pointercancel", up)
  })

  // the smallest reliability each measure could have, given the other one, for the disattenuated correlation to be
  // within -1 to 1
  const minRxx = r * r / ryy, minRyy = r * r / rxx
  const needed = (min, name, other) => min > 1 ? `with measure ${other}'s reliability as ${same ? "reported" : "given"}, no reliability of measure ${name} could bring it within −1 to 1` : `with measure ${other}'s reliability as ${same ? "reported" : "given"}, measure ${name} would need a reliability of at least ${min.toFixed(2)}`
  const [kind, message] = possible
    ? ["ok", same
      ? `<strong>Possible.</strong> Correcting for unreliability changes the correlation from ${fmt(r)} to ${fmt(dis)}, which is within −1 to 1.`
      : `<strong>Plausible.</strong> Correcting for unreliability changes the correlation from ${fmt(r)} to ${fmt(dis)}, which is within −1 to 1. With these typical reliabilities, correlations up to about ${ceiling.toFixed(2)} in size are to be expected.`]
    : same
      ? ["bad", `<strong>Not possible.</strong> The disattenuated correlation is ${fmt(dis)}, outside −1 to 1, so the reported correlation and reliabilities cannot all be correct for the same sample. For a correlation of ${fmt(r)}, the product of the reliabilities must be at least ${(r * r).toFixed(2)}: ${needed(minRxx, 1, 2)}; ${needed(minRyy, 2, 1)}.`]
      : ["warn", `<strong>Implausible.</strong> The disattenuated correlation is ${fmt(dis)}, outside −1 to 1. Because the reliabilities come from other samples, this does not show that the reported correlation is impossible: it would require the measures to have been more reliable in this sample than is typical for them. For a correlation of ${fmt(r)}, the product of the reliabilities in this sample must be at least ${(r * r).toFixed(2)}: ${needed(minRxx, 1, 2)}; ${needed(minRyy, 2, 1)}.`]
  const feedback = html`<div class="sb-feedback sb-feedback-${kind}">`
  feedback.innerHTML = message
  const note = html`<div class="dc-note">The values are used exactly as entered, without allowing for rounding, so treat the result as an intuition pump rather than a formal test.</div>`
  return html`${tiles}${plot}${feedback}${note}`
}
```

Try a correlation of .80 with both reliabilities at .70: the disattenuated correlation is 1.14. Then raise either reliability until the correlation becomes possible. Negative correlations work the same way, against the lower bound of −1.

Some points to keep in mind when using this check:

- **Reliabilities from other samples are still informative.** When an article does not report reliabilities, estimates from a test manual, earlier studies, or a reliability generalization meta-analysis can stand in for them, and the check becomes a plausibility check. It is often said that reliability is a property of scores in a particular sample rather than of a measure, but this is too strong. Reliability generalization meta-analyses, which pool the reliabilities reported for a measure across many samples, find that reliability varies between samples but that the measure itself also contributes to it [@vachahaase1998]: some measures are reliable in most of the samples in which they are used, and others rarely are. A correlation that would be impossible given a measure's typical reliability is not proof of an error, but it is a useful intuition pump and a fair reason to ask questions.
- **Small excesses can arise from sampling error.** The correlation and the reliabilities are all estimates, and in small samples a disattenuated correlation slightly above 1 can occur by chance even when every reported number is correct. A disattenuated correlation of 1.02 in a sample of 50 is weak evidence of a problem. One of 1.30 in a sample of 500 is strong evidence.
- **Rounding is not taken into account.** The app uses the values exactly as entered. A disattenuated correlation just above 1, calculated from values rounded to two decimal places, may be within rounding of a possible one, so the app is better treated as an intuition pump than as a formal test.
- **The type of reliability matters.** Internal consistency coefficients such as Cronbach's α can underestimate or overestimate reliability, depending on whether their assumptions hold, which changes the disattenuated correlation in turn. When an article reports more than one kind of reliability, check the result with each.
- **A disattenuated correlation close to 1 is itself informative.** Even when it is possible, a disattenuated correlation near 1 suggests that the two measures assess the same construct, which may sit uneasily with an article's claim that they measure distinct things.

## Test yourself

Answer all the questions, then click the button below the quiz to see why each answer is right.

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Means and *SD*s**

1.  A sum score of six items, each rated from 1 to 5, can range from 6 to 30. `r webexercises::torf(TRUE)`
2.  When subgroups together make up a whole sample, the mean of the whole sample must lie between the smallest and largest subgroup means. `r webexercises::torf(TRUE)`
3.  A table reports that 5.1% of a sample were divorced, and 0.0% in every one of the regions that make up the sample. This is possible if some of the regions are small. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
4.  On a 1–7 scale with 30 people, an *SD* of 3.20 is: `r webexercises::mcq(c(answer = "Impossible, whatever the mean", "Possible only if the mean is 4", "Possible at any mean", "Possible only for whole-number data"))`
5.  With whole-number responses, a mean of 2.97 can have an *SD* of 0. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
6.  A reported minimum and maximum can make a small *SD* impossible, even though the same *SD* would be possible if only the scale limits were known. `r webexercises::torf(TRUE)`
7.  A reported Cronbach's *α* can make a large *SD* impossible, even though the same *SD* would be possible without it. `r webexercises::torf(TRUE)`
8.  A reported *SD* that lies within the BRIMMER bounds has been shown to be possible. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`

**Estimates inside confidence intervals**

9.  An estimate that lies outside its own 95% confidence interval is: `r webexercises::mcq(c(answer = "Almost always an error", "Common when intervals are bootstrapped", "Expected for odds ratios", "A sign of p-hacking"))`
10. An odds ratio should lie halfway between the lower and upper bounds of its confidence interval. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
11. An estimate that is inside its interval but not in the middle of it, after allowing for rounding, is proof of an error. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
12. Why should values be entered into the confidence interval app with their trailing zeros? `r webexercises::mcq(c(answer = "The number of decimal places sets how much rounding is allowed for", "The app cannot read numbers without them", "Trailing zeros show that the values are exact", "Values without them are treated as percentages"))`
13. If swapping each estimate with its lower bound puts every estimate in the middle of its interval, the article's values can be used as reported. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`

**Coefficients**

14. An article reports an F1 score of 2.76, alongside a precision of .69 and a recall of .69. The F1 score could be correct. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
15. An adjusted *R*^2^ slightly below zero can be correct. `r webexercises::torf(TRUE)`
16. An ordinary *R*^2^ can be negative when a model fits very badly. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
17. Cronbach's *α* can be negative. `r webexercises::torf(TRUE)`
18. Two measures each have a reliability of .70. What is the largest correlation to expect between them? `r webexercises::mcq(c(answer = ".70", ".49", ".84", "1.00"))`
19. A correlation of .80 is reported between two measures whose reliabilities, taken from their test manuals, are both .70. This shows that the correlation is impossible. `r webexercises::torf(FALSE)`
:::

`r webexercises::hide("Why is each answer right?")`

1.  **True.** The range of a sum score is the number of items times the lowest and highest response options: 6 × 1 = 6 and 6 × 5 = 30. Work the range out from the items rather than taking it from the article, which may describe it inconsistently (@sec-mean-inside-range).
2.  **True.** The mean of the whole sample is a weighted average of the subgroup means, so it cannot be smaller than all of them or larger than all of them. The same is true of percentages (@sec-mean-inside-range).
3.  **False.** However small or large the regions are, a percentage for the whole sample cannot be larger than the percentages in every one of the groups that make it up. If every region has 0.0%, so must the whole sample (@sec-mean-inside-range).
4.  **Impossible, whatever the mean.** With 30 people on a 1–7 scale, no *SD* can exceed 3.05, which is reached with half the people at each end of the scale (@sec-sd-bounds).
5.  **False.** An *SD* of 0 means that everyone had the same score, and identical whole numbers cannot have a mean with a fractional part, such as 2.97. Whole-number data raise the floor above zero at every mean that is not a whole number (@sec-sd-bounds).
6.  **True.** A sample that includes both the observed minimum and the observed maximum cannot have a very small *SD*. On a 1–7 scale with 30 people and a mean of 2.97, reporting a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 6 raises the floor from 0.14 to 0.71 (@sec-sd-bounds).
7.  **True.** A reported *α* limits how much the items can disagree with one another, which lowers the ceiling on the *SD* of the total or mean score (@sec-sd-bounds).
8.  **False.** BRIMMER is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. A reported *SD* inside the bounds may still not correspond to any real set of whole-number scores; only BRIMMEST settles that (@sec-sd-bounds, @sec-combined).
9.  **Almost always an error.** For almost every method used in practice, a confidence interval contains its own estimate. The exceptions are rare, and an article that used one would be expected to say so (@sec-estimate-inside-ci).
10. **False.** Intervals for ratios are usually calculated on the log scale, so the estimate lies halfway between the bounds on that scale: it is the geometric mean of the bounds, not their arithmetic mean (@sec-estimate-centred-ci).
11. **False.** Many legitimate methods produce asymmetric intervals, such as profile likelihood, exact, Wilson, and bootstrap intervals. Whether an off-centre estimate is a concern depends on the metric and on the method the article used (@sec-estimate-centred-ci).
12. **The number of decimal places sets how much rounding is allowed for.** A bound reported as 0.30 could have been anything from 0.295 to 0.305, but one entered as 0.3 could have been anything from 0.25 to 0.35 (@sec-estimates-in-cis).
13. **False.** Even if the columns were simply swapped, readers and meta-analysts usually take reported values at face value, and a meta-analyst who uses the wrong estimate or calculates the wrong standard error will distort the pooled results (@sec-estimates-in-cis).
14. **False.** The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it must lie between them, and like them between 0 and 1. With a precision and recall of .69, the F1 score is .69 (@sec-coefficient-bounds).
15. **True.** Adjusted *R*^2^ is bias-corrected, and can fall slightly below zero when *R*^2^ is close to zero. Its lower bound depends on the number of predictors and the sample size, and is usually close to zero (@sec-coefficient-bounds).
16. **False.** *R*^2^ is a proportion of variance, so it lies between 0 and 1. A reported *R*^2^ below zero cannot be correct (@sec-coefficient-bounds).
17. **True.** Cronbach's *α* has no lower bound, and is negative when the items are on average negatively correlated, usually because reverse-keyed items were not reverse-scored. A negative *α* is possible, but a sign of a problem with the scale or its scoring (@sec-coefficient-bounds).
18. **.70.** The largest correlation to expect is the square root of the product of the reliabilities: √(.70 × .70) = .70, however closely related the constructs are (@sec-disattenuation).
19. **False.** The disattenuated correlation would be 1.14, but because the reliabilities come from other samples, this is a plausibility check, not a possibility check: the measures may have been more reliable in this sample. It is a good reason to ask questions, but not proof of an error (@sec-disattenuation).

`r webexercises::unhide()`
